title: Matching a Honey Bottle to an Existing Cap
imageCaption: Bottle and cap options prepared during the customer’s sourcing discussion.
summary: We matched a honey bottle to caps the customer had already purchased locally and completed the bottle, closure and delivered-cost plan.
facts: Existing lid versus a complete new pack
Bottle, cap and delivered-cost plan completed
sections: What the Customer Needed

A honey business contacted us after purchasing caps from a local supplier. The customer wanted a compatible plastic honey bottle, an appropriate capacity for the intended honey weight and an estimate of the delivered cost.
How We Narrowed the Bottle Size

We first separated the requested honey net weight from the bottle’s water-volume rating. This allowed us to shortlist a bottle with enough working capacity and headspace instead of selecting a nominal milliliter size that could overflow when filled with honey.
Checking the Existing Cap

We asked for the existing cap specification because appearance alone cannot confirm thread and sealing compatibility. The discussion then covered two routes: supply the bottle for testing with the customer’s cap, or quote a complete bottle-and-cap assembly from us, including a dispensing-valve option.
The Options We Prepared

We separated the bottle, matching closure and delivery arrangement, then compared local consolidation with direct-delivery considerations. This gave the customer a complete cost basis rather than an isolated bottle unit price.
The Completed Solution

The project concluded with a defined bottle route, a compatible-cap verification plan and a complete delivered-cost comparison. The customer could proceed with the selected configuration knowing which components, fit checks and delivery costs were included.
What This Project Demonstrated

The customer’s target honey weight, existing-cap information, quantity and destination allowed us to compare a bottle-only route with a matched complete pack. This kept the technical decision and the delivered cost connected throughout the project.

title: Selecting 250 ml and 320 ml Honey Bear Bottles
imageCaption: The 250 ml and 320 ml bear bottle formats compared for one customer project.
summary: We helped a customer establish two related honey pack sizes using our 250 ml and 320 ml PET bear bottles.
sections: The Customer’s Pack Plan

The customer was considering two related honey pack sizes and wanted to keep the familiar bear-bottle appearance across both. We shortlisted our 250 ml and 320 ml PET bear bottles so the capacities, proportions and presentation could be compared together.
Capacity and Reference Fill

We provided the catalog capacities together with reference honey fills: approximately 350 g for the 250 ml bottle and 450 g for the 320 ml bottle. We made clear that the final net weight and headspace still had to be confirmed with the customer’s honey and chosen fill level.
Adapting the Label to Both Bears

Both bottles kept the molded bear visible around the front panel, but their usable label areas were not identical. We recommended preparing a separate actual-size artwork proof for each bottle rather than shrinking one label file and assuming it would sit correctly on both curved bodies.
Keeping the Closure Consistent

Both shortlisted bottles use a 38-400 neck finish, which gave the project a practical route to a consistent closure appearance. Even with the same listed finish, we treated each bottle, cap, liner and seal as an assembly to be checked before approval.
The Two-Size Solution

The completed comparison gave the customer two defined bottle formats, reference fill weights and a consistent closure direction. Each size also had its own label-panel requirements, keeping the two packs visually related without forcing one artwork size onto both bottles.
Project Result
The customer finished the project with a coordinated 250 ml and 320 ml bear-bottle range, clear reference fills, a shared neck-finish direction and separate label specifications for the two bodies.

title: Preparing a 25 ml Glass Honey Jar for Export
imageCaption: The 25 ml round glass jar and metal lid selected for the project.
summary: We completed a 25 ml glass honey jar specification with its matching metal lid, label area and protective export packing.
sections: The Requested Jar Format

The customer needed a compact glass container for a small honey portion. We selected our 25 ml round jar as the project reference and paired it with the available metal lid so the container could be assessed as a complete unit.
Dimensions We Confirmed

For the packing layout, we used the assembled reference dimensions of 40.5 mm overall height with the cap and a 40 mm body diameter. These dimensions established the space needed around each jar for dividers and protective material.
Working with the Small Label Area

The jar body provided limited space, so we treated the front label as an actual-size artwork task rather than a scaled-down version of a larger jar label. The lid could carry an additional sticker if the customer needed more visible brand information.
Matching the Metal Lid

We paired the jar with its metal cap option and identified the liner, seal and filling-temperature checks that would be required on the assembled sample. This kept the closure decision connected to the customer’s actual filling process.
Planning the Export Carton

The standard packing reference was 280 jars per carton. Because the container is glass, we also allowed for dividers and protective materials rather than calculating freight from the jar count alone. Final carton dimensions and pallet requirements would be locked with the approved packing method.
The Completed Pack Specification
The completed project brought the 25 ml jar, matching metal lid, assembled dimensions, label approach, carton count and glass protection into one pack specification for export.
